animals.blurb: North America's largest frog, with a distinctive 'jug-o-rum' call that echoes across summer ponds. They eat anything they can fit in their mouths, including other frogs, birds, and snakes.
animals.hint: The largest frog calling 'jug-o-rum' at summer ponds

animals.blurb: Often confused with bullfrogs, green frogs are smaller with distinctive ridges down their backs. Their call sounds like a plucked banjo string.
animals.hint: A pond frog with a twangy banjo-string call

animals.blurb: Named for their leopard-like spots, these frogs wander far from water in summer meadows. Once abundant, they have declined dramatically in western regions.
animals.hint: A spotted meadow frog that wanders far from water

animals.blurb: The only frog found north of the Arctic Circle, wood frogs can survive being frozen solid in winter. Their distinctive black mask looks like a robber's disguise.
animals.hint: A masked forest frog that survives being frozen

animals.blurb: Tiny but mighty, spring peepers announce spring with a chorus of high-pitched whistles that can be deafening. They have an X-shaped marking on their backs.
animals.hint: A tiny tree frog with a mighty spring chorus

animals.blurb: Master of camouflage, gray treefrogs can change from gray to green. Their loud, trilling call is common on summer nights. Toe pads let them climb almost any surface.
animals.hint: A color-changing tree climber with sticky toe pads

animals.blurb: The most commonly heard frog on the West Coast, their 'rib-bit' call is the default frog sound in movies. Despite being called treefrogs, they mostly live on the ground.
animals.hint: The 'rib-bit' frog you hear in Hollywood movies

animals.blurb: A garden ally that eats thousands of insects each summer. Their long, musical trills are a sound of spring. The warty skin secretes mild toxins but won't give you warts.
animals.hint: A warty garden friend with a long musical trill

animals.blurb: Similar to American toads but with a shorter, nasal call like a sheep's bleat. They prefer sandier habitats and have three or more warts per dark spot.
animals.hint: A sandy-habitat toad that bleats like a sheep

animals.blurb: A prairie specialist that breeds explosively after summer rains. Their metallic, jackhammer-like call can be heard from great distances.
animals.hint: A prairie toad with a jackhammer call

animals.blurb: Famous for their three-stage life cycle: aquatic larva, terrestrial red eft, then aquatic adult. The bright orange eft stage can last up to 3 years.
animals.hint: A newt with a bright orange land-dwelling teenager phase

animals.blurb: Large, striking salamanders with bold yellow spots on a black body. They emerge on rainy spring nights to breed in woodland pools, creating an event called the 'Big Night.'
animals.hint: A black salamander with bold yellow polka dots

animals.blurb: One of the largest land salamanders in North America, reaching 14 inches. Their yellow-and-black tiger stripes are unmistakable. They spend most of their lives underground.
animals.hint: A large striped salamander that lives mostly underground

animals.blurb: The most abundant vertebrate in many eastern forests—biomass exceeds all birds and mammals combined. They are lungless and breathe entirely through their skin.
animals.hint: A tiny lungless salamander found under forest logs

animals.blurb: A fully aquatic salamander that never loses its external gills, remaining in a larval-like state throughout life. They were named for the false belief that they bark.
animals.hint: A permanent water-dweller with feathery red gills

animals.blurb: North America's largest salamander, reaching 2 feet long. Their flattened shape and wrinkly skin help them absorb oxygen. They require pristine water and are declining.
animals.hint: A giant wrinkly salamander in clear mountain streams

animals.blurb: One of the most toxic amphibians in North America, producing the same neurotoxin as pufferfish. Their bright orange belly warns predators of their toxicity.
animals.hint: A toxic western newt with an orange warning belly

animals.blurb: A small, robust salamander found along rocky streams. Unlike most salamanders, they can jump to escape predators. Males guard eggs until hatching.
animals.hint: A stream-edge salamander that can jump to escape

animals.blurb: Striking black salamanders with bold white (female) or gray (male) crossbands. Unlike most salamanders, they breed in fall and females guard eggs on land until rains flood the nest.
animals.hint: A black-and-white banded salamander that nests in fall

animals.blurb: An invasive species originally introduced for pest control, cane toads produce potent toxins that kill predators who try to eat them. They can reach 9 inches long.
animals.hint: A giant invasive toad with deadly shoulder glands
